Importance sampling draws particles from a proposal $q$ and corrects for not
sampling from the target $\pi$ with the weight

$$
w(z) = \frac{\pi(z)}{q(z)}, \qquad
\mathbb{E}_\pi[f] = \mathbb{E}_q[w f].
$$

Working out $w$ by hand means writing both densities in their factorised
forms, cancelling what they share, and dropping anything that does not vary
across particles. That last step gives *self-normalised* weights, used when
the target is a posterior known only up to its evidence. `importance_weight`
does these steps symbolically and records each one, so the result can be
checked exactly on a discrete network and, for models, compiled to a
log-weight function.

```{julia}
#| output: false
using PracticalProbability
using Distributions
using Random
rng = Xoshiro(1)
```

## Likelihood weighting

The simplest proposal is the prior. A proposal can use terms of the target's
own distribution `P`, and identical terms cancel:

```{julia}
@rv θ Y
g = @dag θ → Y
lw = importance_weight(P(θ | Y), P(θ); dag = g)
```

The posterior is written in the graph's factorisation. Its normaliser
$\sum_\theta P(\theta)\,P(Y \mid \theta) = P(Y)$ depends only on the data, so
it is dropped, and the prior cancels. What remains is the likelihood.

```{julia}
latex(lw; env = :display)
```

## A proposal of its own

A different proposal is a separate named distribution. `@density q` declares
it, and `q(θ)` never cancels against `P(θ)`:

```{julia}
@density q
iw = importance_weight(P(θ | Y), q(θ); dag = g)
```

## Checking it exactly

On discrete networks every claim can be checked by enumeration: every step of
the derivation, the identity $q \cdot w = \pi$, and that $q$ covers the
target's support. Each named distribution gets its own network.

```{julia}
bn = rand_bayesnet(g; card = 4, rng)
nets = Dict(:P => bn, :q => BayesNet(θ => [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4]))
verify(iw, nets), check_support(iw, nets)
```

A proposal that puts no mass where the target has some fails the support
check:

```{julia}
holey = Dict(:P => bn, :q => BayesNet(θ => [0.5, 0.5, 0.0, 0.0]))
check_support(iw, holey)
```

`relative_ess` is $\mathbb{E}_q[w]^2 / \mathbb{E}_q[w^2]$, the effective
sample size per particle. It is computed exactly, here for the observation
$Y = 1$. The posterior itself is the best possible proposal:

```{julia}
y1 = Y(1)
proposals = ["prior P(θ)" => P(θ), "q(θ)" => q(θ), "posterior P(θ | Y=1)" => P(θ | y1)]
[name => relative_ess(importance_weight(P(θ | y1), prop; dag = g), nets)
 for (name, prop) in proposals]
```

## Sequential Monte Carlo

In a state-space model, a particle filter extends each particle from $X_1$
to $X_2$ and reweights it by the *incremental* weight. The incremental target
is $P(X_2 \mid X_1)\,P(Y_2 \mid X_2)$. The observation $Y_2$ is data, but the
previous state $X_1$ varies across particles and must stay in the weight.

```{julia}
@rv X1 X2 Y1 Y2
h = @dag begin
    X1 → (X2, Y1)
    X2 → Y2
end
target = P(X2 | X1) * P(Y2 | X2)
```

The **bootstrap filter** proposes from the transition kernel, and the weight
is the likelihood of the new observation:

```{julia}
importance_weight(target, P(X2 | X1); dag = h, data = [Y2])
```

The **locally optimal proposal** conditions on the new observation. Its
weight is the predictive likelihood $P(Y_2 \mid X_1)$, which doesn't depend on
the new state at all:

```{julia}
opt = importance_weight(target, P(X2 | X1, Y2); dag = h, data = [Y2])
```

With **any other kernel**, nothing cancels:

```{julia}
importance_weight(target, q(X2 | X1, Y2); dag = h, data = [Y2])
```

The locally optimal weight has no variance given $X_1$: its relative ESS is 1
for every previous state and observation.

```{julia}
bnh = rand_bayesnet(h; card = 3, rng)
extrema(relative_ess(opt, bnh).values)
```

The bootstrap's is lower, and how much lower depends on the previous state
and the observation:

```{julia}
boot = importance_weight(target, P(X2 | X1); dag = h, data = [Y2])
relative_ess(boot, bnh)
```

### Whole paths, on plates

The same step can be written for any time $t$, with indexed variables.
The path target is the joint density of states and observations up to $t$,
a product over a plate. Here `x[0]` is the initial state:

```{julia}
@rv x y
@index t 1:T
@index s 1:t
γ = ∏(s, P(x[s] | x[s-1]) * P(y[s] | x[s]))
```

`smc_weight` derives the incremental weight
$w_t = \gamma_t / (\gamma_{t-1}\, q_t)$. Peeling the last step off $\gamma_t$
cancels the whole past, so only one time slice remains:

```{julia}
smc_weight(γ, P(x[t] | x[t-1]))
```

The locally optimal kernel needs that slice's graph, which is read from the
factors of the last step:

```{julia}
opt_t = smc_weight(γ, P(x[t] | x[t-1], y[t]))
```

The last line is the weight of a whole path, the product of the incremental
weights. To check the derivation exactly at a concrete time, unroll it onto a
network over `x_0, x_1, …`:

```{julia}
gT = DAG([x[0], x[1], x[2], x[3], y[1], y[2], y[3]],
         Dict(x[1] => [x[0]], x[2] => [x[1]], x[3] => [x[2]],
              y[1] => [x[1]], y[2] => [x[2]], y[3] => [x[3]]))
verify(opt_t, rand_bayesnet(gT; card = 3, rng); at = 1:3)
```

## Generative models

The same algebra works on models. `@generative` reads a model's `~`
statements. Put `@graphical` in front of a PracticalBayes or Turing `@model`
to do the same while defining it. The proposal is a second model over the
same latent variables. A `~` statement that is identical in both models,
along with the deterministic assignments it reads, is the same factor and
cancels.

```{julia}
linreg = @generative function linreg(x, y)
    α ~ Normal(0, 10)
    β ~ Normal(0, 10)
    σ ~ Exponential(1)
    μ = α .+ β .* x
    y .~ Normal.(μ, σ)
end

prior_q = @generative function prior_q()
    α ~ Normal(0, 10)
    β ~ Normal(0, 10)
    σ ~ Exponential(1)
end

importance_weight(linreg, prior_q)
```

A proposal centred near the posterior for the regression coefficients keeps
the prior on $\sigma$, so only the coefficients' factors survive:

```{julia}
centred_q = @generative function centred_q()
    α ~ Normal(1, 0.15)
    β ~ Normal(2, 0.25)
    σ ~ Exponential(1)
end

iw_c = importance_weight(linreg, centred_q)
```

`logweight` compiles the surviving factors into a function. It contains only
the factors that didn't cancel, written with each model's own distributions:

```{julia}
logweight_expr(iw_c) |> Base.remove_linenums!
```

### Running it

Draw particles from each proposal, weight them, and estimate the posterior
mean of $\beta$ by self-normalised importance sampling:

```{julia}
xs = collect(range(0, 1; length = 30))
ys = 1 .+ 2 .* xs .+ 0.3 .* randn(rng, length(xs))
data = (x = xs, y = ys)

function snis(iw, draw; n = 20_000)
    logw = @logweight(iw)
    θs = [draw() for _ in 1:n]
    lw = [logw(θ, data) for θ in θs]
    w = exp.(lw .- maximum(lw))
    w ./= sum(w)
    (E_β = sum(w .* getproperty.(θs, :β)), ess = 1 / sum(abs2, w))
end

draw_prior() = (α = rand(rng, Normal(0, 10)), β = rand(rng, Normal(0, 10)), σ = rand(rng, Exponential(1)))
draw_centred() = (α = rand(rng, Normal(1, 0.15)), β = rand(rng, Normal(2, 0.25)), σ = rand(rng, Exponential(1)))

(prior = snis(importance_weight(linreg, prior_q), draw_prior),
 centred = snis(iw_c, draw_centred))
```

Both estimates target the same posterior, but the prior wastes almost every
particle. The weights are correct by construction in both cases. Only the
proposal changes how many particles count.
